requirements.requirement: Curl package is version-locked/held at its currently installed version on node1
requirements.summary: Installed curl was identified as 7.76.1-40.el9. The versionlock dnf plugin (not present by default) was installed and a versionlock entry curl-0:7.76.1-40.el9.* was added, confirmed present in both `dnf versionlock list` and /etc/dnf/plugins/versionlock.list.

requirements.requirement: The hold actually prevents curl from being updated during a system update, even though a newer version is available
requirements.summary: A newer curl build (7.76.1-40.el9_8.5) was confirmed present in the repo. `dnf update curl -y` reported 'Nothing to do', and a simulated full-system update (tsflags=test) showed libcurl upgrading while curl was excluded from the upgrade set, directly demonstrating the lock takes effect during a broader update. rpm -q confirmed the installed curl version was unchanged afterward.

requirements.requirement: Hold persists and curl remains pinned after a node restart
requirements.summary: This is not an explicit part of the task instruction but was demonstrated by the executor: pre-restart boot_id and curl/versionlock state were captured, the node was rebooted with acknowledgement returned before disconnect, connection loss and a new boot_id were observed on return, and post-reboot rpm -q plus dnf versionlock list confirmed curl remained at 7.76.1-40.el9 with the lock rule intact. Fixed lifecycle snapshots independently corroborate the boot_id change (fbdf5b2c... -> f467bb60...) and show no failed services or package-health regressions after executor work.

overall_summary: The executor correctly installed the versionlock plugin and pinned curl to its currently installed version, then directly proved the hold works by showing dnf skip curl during both a targeted update attempt and a simulated full-system update where a newer curl build was available and libcurl still upgraded normally. It additionally ran a full pre/post reboot cycle demonstrating persistence of the hold across a boot-identity change, which is corroborated by the fixed lifecycle snapshots (no failed services, no package-health regressions). All material outcomes of the task are satisfied with direct evidence.
limitations: A trivial /tmp/reboot.log file was left behind by the backgrounded reboot command; low-risk and does not affect functionality.

Evidence for the restart cross-check relies on connection-loss timing plus a boot_id comparison rather than a dedicated service-health check specific to curl functionality post-reboot beyond `curl --version`, though this is sufficient given curl has no running service component.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands trace clearly to the task or to the restart evidence protocol: installing the versionlock plugin and adding the lock (required outcome), a real `dnf update curl -y` attempt (bounded, confirms the hold with no unwanted change since it was a no-op), a dry-run full-update simulation using tsflags=test (does not commit any transaction, so no real mutation occurred), and the reboot itself (part of the fixed restart protocol, executed via a backgrounded sleep+reboot to capture the acknowledgement, which is a reasonable low-risk technique). The only minor residue is /tmp/reboot.log, a small leftover log file from the backgrounded reboot command (cmd-932df18e4f4246ed) visible in the after-executor temporary-files snapshot; this is trivial, non-destructive, and does not affect package or service state. No failed services, no listening-socket changes beyond the expected sshd pid change from the reboot, and package-health checks are clean before and after.
